chapters.title: Follow oxidation numbers, not just oxygen
chapters.formula: Oxidation: increase; reduction: decrease; sum of oxidation numbers = total charge
chapters.script: Welcome to Redox and Electrochemistry. This recorded Chemistry class uses an AI generated Marin voice. Oxidation raises oxidation number, while reduction lowers it. The oxidizing agent accepts electrons and is itself reduced. The reducing agent supplies electrons and is itself oxidized. No oxygen atom is required for a redox reaction: zinc can transfer electrons directly to copper ions. Oxidation numbers sum to the overall species charge. An element in its elemental form has oxidation number zero. Oxygen is usually minus two, but in a peroxide it is minus one. Hydrogen is usually plus one, but in metal hydrides it is minus one. Fluorine in its compounds is minus one. For permanganate, four oxygens contribute minus eight, and the ion's total charge is minus one. Manganese must therefore be plus seven. Reduction to manganese two plus requires five electrons per manganese. Reduction to manganese dioxide instead ends at plus four and requires three. The final product fixes the electron count. In a balanced redox equation, electrons lost equal electrons gained. Assign oxidation numbers first, identify the two changes, and then use electron balance to establish the stoichiometric ratio.

board.heading: The product fixes the electron count

chapters.title: Balance atoms and charge separately
chapters.script: To balance redox half reactions in acidic medium, balance the main element, oxygen with water, hydrogen with hydrogen ions, and charge with electrons. For permanganate becoming manganese two plus, place four waters on the product side, eight hydrogen ions on the reactant side, and five electrons on the reactant side. Iron two plus loses one electron to form iron three plus. Multiply its half reaction by five and add. The combined equation consumes one permanganate, eight hydrogen ions and five iron two plus ions. It produces one manganese two plus, four waters and five iron three plus ions. Both sides have total charge plus seventeen. Thus zero point zero two zero zero moles of permanganate require zero point one zero zero moles of iron two plus. In basic medium with manganese dioxide as the specified product, the balanced reduction consumes one permanganate, two waters and three electrons, forming one manganese dioxide and four hydroxide ions. Each side has one manganese, six oxygen and four hydrogen atoms, with charge minus four. Zero point zero two zero zero moles now require zero point zero six zero zero moles of electrons. Do not copy the acidic five electron count into a reaction with a different product.

board.heading: Balance atoms AND charge

chapters.title: Conductivity and molar conductivity answer different questions
chapters.formula: G = 1/R; kappa = G(l/A); Lambda_m = 1000 kappa/c with the stated units
chapters.script: Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance. Conductivity removes the effect of sample geometry: multiply conductance by the cell constant, which is electrode separation divided by area. Molar conductivity compares conductivity with molar concentration. With conductivity in siemens per centimetre and concentration in moles per litre, molar conductivity is one thousand times conductivity divided by concentration, in siemens centimetres squared per mole. The factor one thousand comes from the volume unit conversion. Consider resistance two hundred ohms, cell constant one point two zero per centimetre, and concentration zero point zero five zero zero molar. Conductance is zero point zero zero five zero zero siemens. Conductivity is zero point zero zero six zero zero siemens per centimetre. Molar conductivity is one hundred twenty siemens centimetres squared per mole. On dilution, conductivity usually falls because a unit volume contains fewer ions, while molar conductivity rises as interionic effects decrease and, for weak electrolytes, ionization increases. These trends refer to different quantities and are not contradictory. At infinite dilution, Kohlrausch's law adds the limiting ionic contributions with their stoichiometric coefficients. A salt releasing two identical anions contributes that anion term twice. Always write the units before using a numerical conductivity formula.

board.heading: Geometry and concentration matter

chapters.title: Build a cell by separating two reactions
chapters.formula: Zn | Zn2+ || Cu2+ | Cu; external electrons: anode -> cathode
points: External electrons · Zinc → copper · Bridge: ions
chapters.script: A galvanic cell separates oxidation and reduction so electrons can pass through an external circuit. In a Daniell cell, zinc loses electrons at the anode, and copper ions gain them at the cathode. Electrons flow through the wire from zinc to copper. The salt bridge carries ions that maintain charge balance; electrons do not travel through its solution. Anode means oxidation and cathode means reduction in both galvanic and electrolytic cells. In a functioning galvanic cell the anode is negative and cathode positive. An external power supply drives an electrolytic cell, whose electrode polarities differ, but those reaction based definitions remain. Cell notation conventionally places the anode on the left and cathode on the right. A single line marks a phase boundary, while a double line represents the electrolyte junction. Standard reduction potentials are measured relative to a reference electrode, conventionally the standard hydrogen electrode. A single isolated electrode potential is not measured without a comparison. Before calculating voltage, write the oxidation and reduction processes and balance their electrons. A correct subtraction formula cannot rescue a reaction whose anode and cathode were assigned inconsistently.

board.heading: Daniell galvanic cell

chapters.title: Subtract reduction potentials without scaling them
chapters.script: Using standard reduction potentials, the standard cell voltage equals the cathode potential minus the anode potential. Copper two plus to copper has the illustrative value plus zero point three four volts, while zinc two plus to zinc has minus zero point seven six. Their difference is plus one point one zero volts. Do not multiply electrode potentials when multiplying half reactions to balance electrons. Voltage is an intensive quantity. Gibbs energy change for the balanced reaction equals minus n times Faraday's constant times reversible cell voltage. Here n is two. With Faraday's constant approximately ninety six thousand five hundred coulombs per mole, the standard Gibbs energy change is minus two hundred twelve point three kilojoules per mole of reaction as written. Doubling the entire reaction doubles n and the Gibbs energy change, while leaving voltage unchanged. Combining this relationship with standard Gibbs energy equals minus R T times natural log K gives natural log K equals n F times standard voltage divided by R T. A positive standard cell voltage therefore implies K greater than one. At reaction equilibrium the actual voltage is zero, while the standard voltage need not be zero. Keep the standard state separate from the present composition.

board.heading: Potentials are not multiplied

chapters.title: The mixture changes the voltage
chapters.formula: At 298 K: E = E_standard - (0.05916/n) log10 Q
chapters.script: The Nernst equation corrects the standard voltage for the current mixture. Cell voltage equals standard voltage minus R T divided by n F, multiplied by the natural logarithm of the reaction quotient Q. For a base ten logarithm at approximately two hundred ninety eight kelvin, the coefficient is about zero point zero five nine one six volts divided by n. For zinc reacting with copper two plus, Q is approximately zinc ion concentration divided by copper ion concentration in the ideal dilute model. Pure solid metals are omitted. With zinc ions at zero point one zero molar and copper ions at one point zero molar, Q is zero point one zero. Its logarithm is minus one. With n equal to two and standard voltage one point one zero volts, subtracting the negative correction gives approximately one point one three volts. In the opposite concentration ratio, Q equal to ten lowers the voltage to about one point zero seven volts. Use dimensionless activities for the rigorous expression, and the stated ideal approximation for these examples. At equilibrium, Q equals K and actual reversible voltage is zero. A concentration cell can have zero standard voltage but a nonzero actual voltage because its two sides have different activities.

board.heading: Nernst: n = 2, E° = 1.10 V

chapters.title: Count charge to predict deposited mass
chapters.formula: Q_electric = It; deposited mass m = MIt/(zF), at 100 percent current efficiency
chapters.script: Electrolysis calculations begin with charge, not voltage. Charge passed is current times time in seconds. Divide by Faraday's constant to obtain moles of electrons. Divide again by the electrons required per product particle, then multiply by molar mass. Copper two plus requires two electrons to produce one copper atom. Suppose two point zero zero amperes flow for four thousand eight hundred twenty five seconds. The charge is nine thousand six hundred fifty coulombs. With Faraday's constant ninety six thousand five hundred coulombs per mole, this supplies zero point one zero zero moles of electrons and can form zero point zero five zero zero moles of copper. Using molar mass sixty three point five grams per mole gives three point one seven five grams, or three point one eight grams to three significant figures. That assumes all current produces the desired copper. At eighty percent current efficiency, multiply by zero point eight zero zero to obtain two point five four grams. Do not divide by the efficiency. Competing reactions reduce the desired yield for a given charge. When several cells carry the same charge, each product amount still depends on its own electron requirement and molar mass.

board.heading: Copper deposition: 2e⁻ per Cu

chapters.title: Batteries store reactants; fuel cells receive them
points: Net chemistry · Acid consumed · Water forms
chapters.script: A primary cell is not designed for normal repeated recharging. The familiar zinc carbon dry cell uses zinc oxidation and manganese dioxide cathode chemistry. Secondary cells are designed for recharging by driving the net chemistry in reverse. During lead acid battery discharge, lead is oxidized at the negative electrode and lead dioxide is reduced at the positive electrode. Both form lead sulfate. The net reaction consumes lead, lead dioxide and two sulfuric acid units, producing two lead sulfate units and two waters. Acid is consumed during discharge. The fact that both electrodes form the same sulfate does not mean both were oxidized: lead changes from zero to plus two, while lead in lead dioxide changes from plus four to plus two. Charging reverses the net chemistry with an external energy supply. A hydrogen oxygen fuel cell receives reactants continuously from outside and produces water overall. Two hydrogen molecules combine with one oxygen molecule to form two waters. Continued operation requires fuel, oxidant and appropriate operating conditions; it is not unlimited energy. Distinguish the storage of reactants inside a battery from their external supply to a fuel cell. Detailed dry cell mechanisms and electrode classifications remain for further study.

board.heading: Lead acid battery: discharge

chapters.title: Infer ionization from conductance
chapters.script: Conductivity can also estimate how much a weak electrolyte ionizes in a suitable dilute model. Divide measured molar conductivity by its limiting molar conductivity to estimate the ionization fraction alpha. Suppose a monoprotic acid has molar conductivity twenty and limiting molar conductivity four hundred, in the same units. The fraction is zero point zero five zero zero, or five percent. For starting concentration zero point zero one zero zero molar, the acid constant is approximately concentration times alpha squared divided by one minus alpha. Substitution gives about two point six three times ten to the minus five in the conventional concentration model. Retaining the denominator accounts for the undissociated fraction. Limiting conductivity may be assembled from limiting ionic contributions using Kohlrausch's law when direct extrapolation for a weak electrolyte is unreliable. This estimate assumes the conductivity ratio is an appropriate measure of ionization and neglects additional activity effects. It is not a universal exact acid constant measurement. Check whether the supplied quantity is conductivity or molar conductivity, whether the units agree, and whether the concentration is in the required units. Use the twelve original quiz questions and seven worked examples to connect these calculations with cells, redox balance and electrolysis.

board.heading: Weak electrolyte conductance model

chapters.title: Concentration cells can have nonzero voltage
chapters.formula: Zn concentration cell at 25 °C: E = (0.05916/2) log10(acathode/aanode)
chapters.script: Two identical metal electrodes can produce a cell voltage when their ion activities differ. Consider zinc electrodes in an ideal dilute model at twenty five degrees Celsius, with zinc ion concentrations zero point zero zero one zero and zero point one zero zero molar. The standard cell voltage is zero because the electrode couples are the same. The actual voltage is not zero: concentration contributes through the Nernst equation. The concentrated compartment acts as the cathode in the spontaneous orientation, consuming zinc ions by reduction. The dilute compartment acts as the anode, producing zinc ions by oxidation. With two electrons transferred, the voltage is zero point zero five nine one six divided by two, times the base ten logarithm of one hundred, giving zero point zero five nine one six volt. The process tends to reduce the concentration difference. Use activities when nonideality matters, and neglect liquid junction contributions only within the stated model. Identical electrode materials therefore do not guarantee identical electrode potentials. Label the compartments and electron direction before writing the concentration ratio, because reversing the cell reverses the voltage sign.
points: Dilute Zn²⁺ side · 0.0010 M · Anode: Zn oxidizes
Concentrated Zn²⁺ side · 0.100 M · Cathode: Zn²⁺ reduces

board.heading: Concentration cells can have nonzero voltage

chapters.title: Connect standard voltage to equilibrium
chapters.script: Standard cell voltage connects electrochemistry with both Gibbs energy and the equilibrium constant. At twenty five degrees Celsius, the base ten logarithm of the dimensionless equilibrium constant equals electron number times standard voltage divided by approximately zero point zero five nine one six volt. Suppose a defined two electron reaction has standard voltage zero point one one eight three two volt. The logarithm is four and the equilibrium constant is ten thousand. The corresponding standard Gibbs energy is minus electron number times the Faraday constant times standard voltage. Using Faraday constant ninety six thousand five hundred coulombs per mole gives about minus twenty two point eight four kilojoules per mole of reaction as written. Doubling a reaction doubles the electron count and Gibbs energy change, but it does not double its electrode voltage. The equilibrium constant for the doubled equation is squared. Actual reaction direction also depends on composition through the reaction quotient. A positive standard voltage is therefore not a guarantee that every possible initial mixture operates spontaneously in the written direction. Keep equation scaling, standard states and actual mixture conditions separate.

board.heading: Connect standard voltage to equilibrium

chapters.title: Use ionic conductances to infer dissociation
chapters.script: Independent ionic migration at infinite dilution allows useful conductance combinations. For a weak monoprotic acid H A, combine the limiting molar conductances of hydrochloric acid and the sodium salt of A, then subtract sodium chloride. The sodium and chloride contributions cancel, leaving hydrogen ion plus A ion. With illustrative values four hundred twenty six, ninety one and one hundred twenty six in compatible conductance units, the result is three hundred ninety one. Suppose a zero point zero one zero zero molar acid has conductivity one point five six four times ten to the minus four siemens per centimetre. Its molar conductivity is one thousand times conductivity divided by concentration, or fifteen point six four siemens square centimetres per mole. Dividing by the limiting value gives an approximate ionized fraction zero point zero four zero. In the simple weak acid model, K a is concentration times alpha squared divided by one minus alpha, about one point six seven times ten to the minus five. This inference assumes the stated dilute solution and ion mobility approximations; activities, water ionization and other dissolved electrolytes can require a fuller treatment.

board.heading: Use ionic conductances to infer dissociation

chapters.title: Same charge does not mean equal metal masses
chapters.script: Cells connected in series receive the same charge, but their deposited masses depend on molar mass and electron stoichiometry. Take one thousand nine hundred thirty coulombs through a copper two ion cell and a silver ion cell. Using Faraday constant ninety six thousand five hundred, the charge corresponds to zero point zero two zero zero mole of electrons. Copper deposition needs two electrons per atom, giving zero point zero one zero zero mole of copper. With illustrative molar mass sixty three point five, the ideal mass is zero point six three five gram. Silver requires one electron per atom, giving zero point zero two zero zero mole and mass two point one five eight grams for molar mass one hundred seven point nine. If only eighty percent of charge produces copper, its deposited mass becomes zero point five zero eight gram. Do not apply that efficiency to a different cell unless specified. Equal current and time establish equal charge, not equal moles of deposited atoms. Check the actual electrode product and electron number before using the equivalent mass ratio.

board.heading: Same charge does not mean equal metal masses

chapters.title: Corrosion is a coupled electrochemical process
chapters.formula: Iron oxidation can couple to oxygen reduction in a moist environment
chapters.script: Corrosion can involve different anodic and cathodic regions on a metal surface. In a common neutral aerated water model, iron oxidizes to iron two ions while oxygen is reduced with water to hydroxide ions. The oxygen half equation consumes four electrons per oxygen molecule and produces four hydroxide ions. Two iron oxidation events supply those four electrons. Further reactions lead to hydrated iron oxide materials commonly called rust; the complete material is not captured by one simple dissolved ion alone. A sacrificial zinc coating or connected zinc piece can preferentially oxidize while electrical contact and suitable environmental conditions are maintained, helping protect iron. A tin coating can serve as a barrier, but a damaged coating exposes a different galvanic situation and does not provide the same sacrificial protection. Do not decide behaviour from a coating's appearance alone. Oxygen supply, moisture, electrical contact and the actual solution affect the process. Distinguish prevention by excluding the environment from prevention by directing oxidation to a more readily oxidized metal. Standard potential tables are a starting guide, not a substitute for the real corrosion conditions.
points: Anodic iron step · Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ · Two events supply 4e⁻
Cathodic oxygen step · O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻ · Neutral aerated model
Sacrificial zinc · Electrical contact matters · Zinc can oxidize first

board.heading: Corrosion is a coupled electrochemical process

chapters.title: Combine electrode steps through Gibbs energies
chapters.script: Electrode potentials cannot generally be added like reaction energies. Consider supplied reduction steps for the same element in one consistent medium. The three plus ion accepts one electron to become the two plus ion, with standard reduction potential plus zero point six zero volt. The two plus ion accepts two electrons to form the metal, with potential minus zero point three zero volt. The overall step transfers three electrons. Convert each potential to standard Gibbs energy using minus n F E, add the two energies, then divide by minus three F. The resulting potential is zero volt, because one times zero point six zero plus two times minus zero point three zero equals zero. The simple arithmetic mean would instead give plus zero point one five volt, which is wrong. All endpoint states and standard-state conventions must match for this cancellation. Zero standard potential means zero standard Gibbs energy for the combined half-reaction relative to the chosen reference, not that every actual mixture is at equilibrium. Composition can still change the electrode potential.
points: M³⁺ + 3e⁻ → M · E°=(0.60−0.60)/3 · 0.00 V; match endpoint states

board.heading: Combine electrode steps through Gibbs energies

chapters.title: Disproportionation oxidizes and reduces one species
chapters.script: Disproportionation converts one oxidation state into both a higher and a lower oxidation state. Use supplied rounded aqueous copper reduction potentials: copper one plus accepting one electron to become copper metal has plus zero point five two volt, and copper two plus accepting one electron to become copper one plus has plus zero point one five volt. Reverse the second half-reaction to oxidize one copper one plus ion. Add it to reduction of another copper one plus ion. The balanced result is two copper one plus ions forming one copper two plus ion and one copper atom. Standard cell potential is zero point five two minus zero point one five, or plus zero point three seven volt. One electron transfers per written reaction, so standard Gibbs energy is minus zero point three seven F. Positive standard voltage favours disproportionation under the stated standard conditions. It does not guarantee the same behaviour in every ligand environment: complexation, precipitation and activities can alter the comparison. Check atom balance, charge balance and the electron count before inferring a redox direction.
points: Reduction: Cu⁺ + e⁻ → Cu · Supplied E°=+0.52 V · Cu(+1) becomes Cu(0)
Oxidation: Cu⁺ → Cu²⁺ + e⁻ · Reverse E°red=+0.15 V · Cu(+1) becomes Cu(+2)
Net: 2Cu⁺ → Cu²⁺ + Cu · 0.52−0.15=+0.37 V · n=1; stated aqueous conditions

board.heading: Disproportionation oxidizes and reduces one species

chapters.title: Hydrogen-electrode potential depends on pH
chapters.formula: At 298 K and pH₂/p°=1: E = −0.05916 pH volts
chapters.script: A hydrogen electrode is at zero standard potential only under its specified standard conditions. Write the reduction as two hydrogen ions plus two electrons forming hydrogen gas. At two hundred ninety eight kelvin, with hydrogen pressure equal to the standard pressure and approximately ideal gas behaviour, the Nernst equation gives potential minus zero point zero five nine one six times p H in volts relative to the standard hydrogen electrode. Thus p H three gives minus zero point one seven seven four eight volt, while p H five gives minus zero point two nine five eight zero volt. The potential difference between these otherwise matched electrodes has magnitude zero point one one eight three two volt. The lower p H side has the more positive reduction potential and acts as the cathode in the ideal cell. This model neglects liquid junction potentials and uses hydrogen ion activities through the definition of p H. A nonstandard gas pressure adds its own term. Always state temperature, gas pressure and reference before treating a measured potential as a p H indicator.

pH 3 versus pH 5 · −0.17748 versus −0.29580 V · Lower pH has higher Ered

chapters.title: Water electrolysis links charge to two gas amounts
chapters.script: Water electrolysis produces different gas amounts at the two electrodes because their electron requirements differ. In a supplied ideal acidified-water model with inert electrodes, the cathode reduces hydrogen ions to hydrogen, while the anode oxidizes water to oxygen. Each hydrogen molecule corresponds to two electrons, and each oxygen molecule to four. Suppose the same circuit passes nineteen thousand three hundred coulombs, using Faraday constant ninety six thousand five hundred coulombs per mole. The electron amount is zero point two zero zero mole. At full current efficiency, hydrogen production is zero point one zero zero mole and oxygen production zero point zero five zero zero mole. At the same temperature and pressure, with approximately ideal gas behaviour, their dry volumes are in ratio two to one. Do not add the electrode electron amounts: the same circuit charge passes through both electrodes. Competing electrode reactions, gas dissolution, leakage and collection over water can change observed amounts or require corrections. This model specifically excludes chloride or other species that could change the anode product. Balance each half-reaction before translating charge into a collected gas amount.
points: Same T and P; ideal dry gases · Volume ratio follows mole ratio · H₂:O₂ = 2:1; full efficiency

board.heading: Water electrolysis links charge to two gas amounts
rows: Same T and P; ideal dry gases

chapters.title: Calibrate the conductivity cell before comparing solutions
chapters.formula: Cell constant = κstandard Rstandard; κunknown = cell constant / Runknown
chapters.script: A measured resistance depends on both the liquid and the electrode geometry. Calibrate the cell with a standard of known conductivity at the stated temperature. Suppose the standard conductivity is zero point zero zero one two zero siemens per centimetre and its measured resistance is one hundred ohms. Multiplying gives cell constant zero point one two zero per centimetre. Now put the unknown solution in the same unchanged cell. A resistance of three hundred ohms gives conductivity zero point zero zero zero four zero zero siemens per centimetre. If its analytical concentration is zero point zero zero two zero zero mole per litre, multiply conductivity by one thousand and divide by that concentration to obtain molar conductivity two hundred siemens square centimetres per mole. Resistance is not simply the reciprocal of conductivity: its reciprocal is conductance, which still contains geometry. The factor one thousand converts the litre concentration convention to the centimetre volume convention. Keep temperature, immersion geometry and units consistent between calibration and measurement. These supplied values illustrate calibration arithmetic rather than certify a particular commercial reference solution.
points: Standard: κ=.00120 S/cm · R = 100 Ω; multiply κR · Cell constant .120 cm⁻¹
c = .00200 mol/L · Λm = 1000κ / c · 200 S cm²/mol

board.heading: Calibrate the conductivity cell before comparing solutions

chapters.title: Changing current requires an area under the curve
chapters.script: Faraday calculations begin with charge, not with a current reading taken at an arbitrary instant. Suppose current rises linearly from two amperes to four amperes during six hundred seconds. The current time area is a rectangle of twelve hundred coulombs plus a triangle of six hundred, giving eighteen hundred coulombs in total. Equivalently, the average of the two endpoint currents is three amperes for this linear ramp. Using the final current for the entire interval would wrongly give twenty four hundred coulombs. In a supplied copper deposition model, only eighty percent of the charge reduces copper two ions to metal; the remainder goes to other electrode processes. Copper receives fourteen hundred forty coulombs. With two electrons per copper atom, Faraday constant ninety six thousand five hundred coulombs per mole and copper molar mass sixty three point five grams per mole, the deposited mass is about zero point four seven four gram. Current efficiency allocates charge, not the number of electrons required by the copper half reaction. An endpoint average is exact for this linear ramp, but a general current trace needs its actual area.
points: Linear ramp: 2 → 4 A · 600 s; mean current 3 A · Total Q = 1800 C
Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu · 80% current efficiency · Cu charge = 1440 C

board.heading: Changing current requires an area under the curve

chapters.title: Alkaline redox balancing must keep hydroxide
chapters.script: Oxidation numbers determine electron exchange, but they do not finish an aqueous equation. In a supplied alkaline model, permanganate is reduced to manganese dioxide while sulfite is oxidized to sulfate. Manganese changes from plus seven to plus four, accepting three electrons per atom. Sulfur changes from plus four to plus six, losing two electrons per atom. The smallest shared electron count is six, so use two permanganates and three sulfites. Completing the basic half reaction balance and cancelling common water and hydroxide gives two permanganates, three sulfites and one water forming two manganese dioxides, three sulfates and two hydroxides. Each side contains two manganese atoms, three sulfur atoms, eighteen oxygen atoms and two hydrogens. Total charge is negative eight on each side. Thus zero point zero two zero zero mole permanganate corresponds to zero point zero three zero zero mole sulfite consumed in this stated net conversion. Do not carry over the five electron acidic permanganate factor: the selected manganese product is different. Medium and endpoint species must be specified before assigning the redox equivalent factor.
points: Mn: +7 → +4; S: +4 → +6 · 3e⁻ accepted; 2e⁻ lost · LCM: 6 electrons
.0200 mol permanganate · Sulfite / permanganate = 3/2 · .0300 mol sulfite

chapters.title: Battery capacity counts electrons and active reactants
chapters.script: Battery capacity in ampere hours is an amount of charge, not an amount of energy. One ampere hour equals three thousand six hundred coulombs. For an ideal lead acid cell discharging by the stated overall reaction, one mole of lead metal and one mole of lead dioxide consume two moles of sulfuric acid while two moles of electrons pass through the external circuit. Thus an ideal one ampere hour discharge corresponds to three thousand six hundred divided by twice the Faraday constant moles of reaction. Using ninety six thousand five hundred coulombs per mole gives about zero point zero one eight seven mole each of lead and lead dioxide consumed, and zero point zero three seven three mole sulfuric acid. The acid is a reactant, not merely an unchanged conducting medium. These are theoretical stoichiometric amounts for one cell under the stated discharge model. Actual usable capacity depends on accessible material, operating conditions and losses. To calculate electrical energy, integrate cell voltage against transferred charge, or use a justified average voltage; an ampere hour rating alone does not supply that voltage.

chapters.title: A copper anode and an inert anode change different inventories
chapters.formula: Cu anode: Cu→Cu²⁺+2e⁻; inert anode: 2H₂O→O₂+4H⁺+4e⁻ in the stipulated sulfate model
chapters.script: The material of an electrode can change the overall electrolysis reaction even when the cathode deposits the same metal. Compare two stipulated copper sulfate cells with enough copper ions, complete copper deposition at the cathode and one thousand nine hundred thirty coulombs passed. With Faraday constant ninety six thousand five hundred, each cell transfers zero point zero two zero zero mole electrons and deposits zero point zero one zero zero mole copper. At a copper anode, oxidation dissolves the same copper amount, so the anode loses zero point six three five gram while the cathode gains that mass for molar mass sixty three point five. The ideal bulk copper ion inventory is replenished. With a suitable inert anode and water oxidation as the only anode reaction, oxygen production is zero point zero zero five zero zero mole and hydrogen ion production zero point zero two zero zero mole. Copper ions are consumed without metal replacement from that anode. Sulfate is a spectator in this model. Electrode labels describe oxidation and reduction, not whether the electrode must always dissolve. Actual competing reactions, current efficiency and solution composition must be checked before applying these ideal inventories.

chapters.title: Aqueous brine does not give the molten-salt products
chapters.formula: Cathode: 2H₂O+2e⁻→H₂+2OH⁻; anode: 2Cl⁻→Cl₂+2e⁻ in the stated brine model
chapters.script: An aqueous sodium chloride cell contains water as a possible reactant, so its products need not match molten sodium chloride. In the stipulated concentrated brine model with suitable electrodes, water reduction gives hydrogen and hydroxide at the cathode rather than deposition of sodium metal. Chloride oxidation gives chlorine at the anode. Adding the half equations cancels electrons and yields two chlorides plus two waters forming one hydrogen molecule, one chlorine molecule and two hydroxides. Sodium ions remain counterions. For zero point one zero zero mole electrons at complete efficiency for those specified products, hydrogen and chlorine amounts are each zero point zero five zero zero mole and hydroxide amount zero point one zero zero mole. These are separate compartment production amounts before crossover or secondary reactions. Chlorine contacting hydroxide can change the final products, so the simple ledger assumes effective separation. The selected anode product depends on concentration, electrode surface and overpotential; a standard potential table alone does not guarantee chlorine under every aqueous condition. This comparison explains a supplied cell's observations and charge balance, rather than providing a procedure for generating or collecting these reactive gases.

chapters.title: Fuel-cell voltage and efficiency use Gibbs energy
chapters.script: A fuel cell's reversible electrical work is linked to Gibbs energy, not automatically to all the heat available from combustion. Use the supplied standard reaction for one mole hydrogen and half a mole oxygen forming one mole liquid water at the stated temperature. Let the reaction Gibbs change be minus two hundred thirty seven kilojoules per mole and the enthalpy change minus two hundred eighty six. Two moles of electrons move through the external circuit per mole hydrogen. Dividing two hundred thirty seven thousand joules by twice Faraday constant ninety six thousand five hundred gives a reversible cell voltage of approximately one point two two eight volts. On the specified liquid water enthalpy basis, the reversible electrical efficiency is two hundred thirty seven divided by two hundred eighty six, approximately eighty two point nine percent. This does not state that every operating device achieves that efficiency. Finite current voltage losses, fuel utilization and auxiliary power can reduce delivered electrical output. Changing temperature or using water vapour and a different heating value changes the comparison. A cell voltage is an energy per charge, while efficiency is a dimensionless ratio with an explicit energy basis.
points: Per H₂: ΔG=−237; ΔH=−286 kJ/mol · n=2; Erev=237000/(2F) · Erev≈1.228 V

chapters.title: Complexation shifts a silver electrode through free ions
chapters.formula: E=E°+0.05916 log₁₀[Ag⁺] at 25°C; [Ag⁺]=CAg/(1+KfL²) in the stipulated ideal model
chapters.script: A metal electrode responds to the activity of the reacting free ion, not automatically the total concentration of every complex containing that metal. Consider silver metal in a stipulated solution at twenty five degrees Celsius, with total dissolved silver zero point zero one zero zero molar and free ammonia held at zero point one zero molar. Use formation constant ten to the seven for the diamminesilver ion, and neglect other complexes, precipitation and activity corrections. Free silver concentration is total silver divided by one plus formation constant times ammonia squared. It is therefore approximately ten to the minus seven molar. For the reduction silver ion plus electron giving silver metal, the Nernst expression is standard potential plus zero point zero five nine one six times the logarithm of free silver concentration relative to one molar. With standard potential zero point eight zero zero volt, the electrode potential is approximately zero point three eight six volt. Using the total zero point zero one zero zero molar instead would incorrectly give about zero point six eight two volt. Complexation lowers the free ion activity here. The resulting electrode potential remains relative to the same reference; it is not a complete cell voltage without a second electrode.

quiz.question: An oxidizing agent is itself:
quiz.explanation: It accepts electrons from another species and is reduced during electron transfer.

quiz.question: Reduction occurs at which electrode in both galvanic and electrolytic cells?
quiz.explanation: Cathode is defined by reduction, regardless of whether an external source drives the cell.

quiz.question: Using +0.34 V and -0.76 V as cathode and anode reduction potentials, E_standard is:
quiz.explanation: Subtract the anode reduction potential: 0.34 - (-0.76) = 1.10 V.

quiz.question: Doubling a balanced cell reaction changes its standard cell voltage by:
quiz.explanation: Both electron amount and Gibbs-energy change double; their ratio defining voltage does not.

quiz.question: At 298 K, lowering Q below one changes E relative to E_standard by:
quiz.explanation: A negative log10 Q makes the subtracted Nernst correction positive.

quiz.question: 9650 C deposits how many moles of Cu from Cu2+ at full efficiency, with F = 96500 C/mol?
quiz.explanation: The charge supplies 0.100 mol electrons; two electrons are needed per copper atom.

quiz.question: When MnO4- reduces to MnO2, electrons accepted per manganese are:
quiz.explanation: Manganese changes from +7 to +4, so three electrons are accepted. The product, not just the reactant, fixes the count.

quiz.question: In MnO4- + 2H2O + 3e- -> MnO2 + xOH-, x equals:
quiz.explanation: Four hydroxides balance four hydrogen atoms, six oxygen atoms in total and net charge minus four.

quiz.question: With R = 200 ohm and cell constant 1.20 cm^-1, conductivity is:
quiz.explanation: Conductance is 0.00500 S. Multiply, not divide, by the cell constant to obtain conductivity.

quiz.question: A weak electrolyte has Lambda_m = 20 and limiting Lambda_m = 400 in the same units. Its estimated ionization fraction is:
quiz.explanation: The dilute model uses alpha = Lambda_m/Lambda_m_infinity = 20/400 = 0.05.

quiz.question: During normal lead-acid battery discharge, the net reaction:
quiz.explanation: Both electrodes form PbSO4 and sulfuric acid is consumed overall; lead oxidizes while lead dioxide is reduced.

quiz.question: An ideal copper deposit is 3.175 g. At 80.0 percent current efficiency, the actual mass is:
quiz.explanation: Multiply the ideal mass by 0.800. Reduced efficiency decreases the desired deposit, not increases it.

quiz.question: For the stated Zn concentration cell at 25 °C, [Zn2+] values 0.0010 and 0.100 M give spontaneous E approximately:
quiz.explanation: The ratio is 100; (0.05916/2)log10(100)=0.05916 V in the spontaneous orientation.

quiz.question: At 25 °C, n=2 and E°=0.11832 V give equilibrium K:
Illustrative limiting molar conductances 426, 91 and 126 combine as Λ∞(HA)=:
quiz.explanation: Add HCl and NaA and subtract NaCl: 426+91−126=391.

quiz.question: With Q=1930 C, F=96500 C/mol, Cu2+ and M(Cu)=63.5 g/mol, ideal copper mass is:
quiz.explanation: 0.0200 mol electrons deposits 0.0100 mol Cu, giving 0.635 g at 100% current efficiency.

quiz.question: At 80% current efficiency for that copper deposition, mass is:
quiz.explanation: Multiply the ideal mass by the specified efficiency: 0.8×0.635=0.508 g.

quiz.question: Sacrificial zinc protection of iron relies on:
options: Preferential zinc oxidation with suitable electrical contact
A coating colour identifying the anode
quiz.explanation: The sacrificial metal can oxidize in place of iron while the galvanic conditions and contact support protection.

quiz.question: Sequential reductions transfer one electron at +0.60 V, then two electrons at −0.30 V. Combined standard potential is:
quiz.explanation: Add standard Gibbs energies, giving the electron-weighted potential (1×0.60+2×−0.30)/3=0.00 V.

quiz.question: The thermodynamic quantity added when combining matched electrode half-reactions is:
quiz.explanation: Gibbs energy is extensive and additive for matched reaction steps; electrode potential is not.

quiz.question: Supplied E°red(Cu+/Cu)=+0.52 V and E°red(Cu2+/Cu+)=+0.15 V. For 2Cu+→Cu2++Cu, E° is:
quiz.explanation: Reduce one Cu+ and oxidize another: 0.52−0.15=+0.37 V for disproportionation.

quiz.question: For that written disproportionation, the electron transfer count n in ΔG°=−nFE° is:
quiz.explanation: One Cu+ loses one electron while another accepts it; n is one for the reaction as written.

quiz.question: At 298 K and standard hydrogen gas pressure, hydrogen electrode potential at pH 3 is:
quiz.explanation: The supplied Nernst form is E=−0.05916 pH V, giving −0.17748 V relative to SHE.

quiz.question: In an ideal hydrogen-electrode cell at pH 3 and pH 5 with equal standard gas pressures, the cathode is:
quiz.explanation: The pH 3 electrode has the more positive reduction potential and is the cathode in this model.

quiz.question: Ideal water electrolysis passes 19300 C with F=96500 C/mol. At full efficiency, hydrogen amount is:
quiz.explanation: The charge is 0.200 mol electrons; forming each H2 molecule requires two electrons, giving 0.100 mol H2.

quiz.question: For that ideal acidified-water electrolysis, the oxygen amount is:
quiz.explanation: Each O2 molecule corresponds to four electrons, so 0.200 mol electrons gives 0.0500 mol O2.

quiz.question: A conductivity standard has κ=.00120 S/cm and R=100 Ω. The calibrated cell constant is:
quiz.explanation: The cell constant equals κR=.00120×100=.120 cm⁻¹.

quiz.question: That cell measures an unknown R=300 Ω at c=.00200 mol/L. Its molar conductivity is:
Current rises linearly from 2 to 4 A over 600 s. Total charge is:
quiz.explanation: The mean current is 3 A for this linear ramp; Q=3×600=1800 C.

quiz.question: For that charge, Cu²⁺ deposition at 80% efficiency with F=96500 C/mol and MCu=63.5 g/mol gives approximately:
quiz.explanation: Only 1440 C deposits copper, so m=1440×63.5/(2×96500)=.474 g.

quiz.question: In the stated alkaline MnO4−→MnO2 and SO3²−→SO4²− model, the permanganate:sulfite coefficient ratio is:
quiz.explanation: Manganese accepts three electrons and sulfur loses two; the smallest common exchange is six.

quiz.question: For .0200 mol MnO4− completely converted to MnO2 in that net model, consumed sulfite is:
quiz.explanation: The balanced ratio SO3²−:MnO4− is 3:2, giving .0300 mol sulfite.

quiz.question: A capacity rating of 1.00 A h corresponds to charge:
quiz.explanation: One hour is 3600 seconds, and one ampere equals one coulomb per second.

quiz.question: For an ideal single lead-acid cell transferring 3600 C on discharge, the stated overall equation predicts H2SO4 consumption approximately:
quiz.explanation: There are two acid molecules per two transferred electrons; acid amount=Q/F≈.0373 mol.

quiz.question: Passing 1930 C through the stipulated CuSO₄ cell with a copper anode and 100% copper efficiency at both electrodes gives (F=96500 C/mol, MCu=63.5 g/mol):
options: Cathode loses .635 g; anode gains .635 g
Cathode gains .635 g; anode loses .635 g
quiz.explanation: The charge is .0200 mol electrons, giving .0100 mol copper deposited at the cathode and dissolved at the copper anode.

quiz.question: With the same charge but an inert anode producing only O₂ by water oxidation, its oxygen amount is:
quiz.explanation: Water oxidation releases four electrons per O₂, so .0200/4=.00500 mol O₂; copper ions are not replenished by that anode.

quiz.question: For the stated concentrated aqueous brine pathways, the cathode product is:
options: Sodium metal as in molten NaCl
quiz.explanation: Water reduction produces H₂ and OH⁻ in this aqueous model, whereas molten NaCl has a different set of available reactants.

quiz.question: At 100% stipulated efficiencies, .100 mol electrons in a separated brine cell forms H₂, Cl₂ and OH⁻ amounts respectively:
quiz.explanation: The half equations require two electrons per H₂ and per Cl₂, while one hydroxide is formed per electron at the cathode.

quiz.question: Per mole H₂ forming liquid water, supplied ΔG=−237 kJ/mol and n=2. With F=96500 C/mol, reversible voltage is approximately:
quiz.explanation: Maximum electrical work magnitude is 237000 J/mol; divide by 2×96500 C/mol to obtain volts.

quiz.question: For the same fuel-cell reaction with ΔH=−286 kJ/mol, the ideal liquid-water enthalpy-basis electrical efficiency is:
quiz.explanation: The reversible ratio is |ΔG|/|ΔH|=237/286≈.829 on this specified enthalpy basis; operating losses can lower delivery.

quiz.question: In the stipulated silver/ammonia model, CAg=.0100 M, Kf=10⁷ and free L=.100 M. Free Ag⁺ concentration is approximately:
quiz.explanation: Divide total dissolved silver by 1+KfL²=100001; the reacting free ion is only a small part of the inventory.

quiz.question: At 25°C with free Ag⁺≈10⁻⁷ M and E°=.800 V, E for Ag⁺+e⁻→Ag is approximately:
quiz.explanation: Use E=.800+.05916 log₁₀(10⁻⁷)=.38588 V relative to the same reference, rather than inserting total silver.
